abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: Drug resistance is a significant challenge in cancer treatment, greatly impacting treatment efficacy. Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) play crucial roles in mediating drug resistance, yet few computational models effectively predict drug resistance-associated ncRNAs. Existing methods often overlook the complex sequence patterns of ncRNA and their intricate interrelationships, resulting in suboptimal performance. To address these challenges, we propose MIFNDRA, a multimodal integrative framework that jointly models ncRNA and drug features to identify drug resistance-related ncRNAs. MIFNDRA employs a pre-trained Graph Isomorphism Network to extract drug structural features and a pre-trained SpliceBERT model to encode ncRNA sequences. It also incorporates various similarity features for both drugs and ncRNAs, while improving representation through a novel ncRNA interaction network that includes interactions between different ncRNA types as a strategy for knowledge enhancement. By leveraging advanced graph learning techniques, including residual GraphSAGE and contrastive learning, the model improves the identification of drug resistance-associated ncRNAs. Additionally, we curated a new benchmark dataset pairing ncRNA sequences with drug SMILES and resistance annotations. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MIFNDRA achieved state-of-the-art performance. Case studies on cisplatin and gemcitabine further validate the model's robustness and potential in advancing drug resistance research and drug development. The data and code required for this work are available at https://github.com/SJNNNN/MIFNDRA.

sec.p: Keywords: ncRNA–drug resistance association prediction, multimodal feature integration, knowledge-enhancement strategy, graph learning, contrastive learning

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Non-coding RNAs (ncRNAs) are DNA-derived transcripts that do not encode proteins and include subclasses such as long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs), microRNAs (miRNAs), circular RNAs (circRNAs), PIWI-interacting RNAs (piRNAs), and small nucleolar RNAs (snoRNAs) [1]. ncRNAs play essential roles in cellular processes including proliferation, apoptosis, and autophagy, and help regulate genomic stability and gene expression from transcription to splicing. Growing evidence shows that ncRNA dysregulation is closely involved in cancer biology, contributing to cancer stem cell initiation, metastasis, and drug resistance, making ncRNAs promising therapeutic targets. However, traditional treatments—surgery, radiotherapy, and chemotherapy—are often undermined by drug resistance, which can drive recurrence, metastasis, and treatment failure [2–4]. High-throughput sequencing studies indicate that resistance is strongly associated with genomic mutations and instability, leading to phenotypic changes that further aggravate resistance. Moreover, aberrant ncRNA expression is implicated in many diseases and actively promotes chemoresistance in cancer cells. Together, these findings underscore the importance of ncRNAs in therapeutic responses and their potential for overcoming drug resistance in cancer therapy [5, 6].

With growing evidence linking ncRNAs to drug resistance, early investigations mainly depended on time-consuming and expensive experimental validation. In contrast, computational approaches enable rapid exploration of ncRNA functions in drug resistance, accelerating research progress. Li et al. [7] proposed LRGCPND, a computational framework utilizing graph convolutional networks (GCNs) and residual learning to uncover latent relationships between ncRNAs and drug resistance. Zheng et al. [8] introduced GSLRDA, which uses a lightweight graph convolutional network (lightGCN) and data augmentation techniques to predict ncRNA-drug resistance associations through contrastive learning. Zhang et al. [9] developed B-NDRA, a framework that constructs a heterogeneous graph and combines attention mechanisms, graph neural networks, and dual adaptive deep adjustment architectures to predict associations using a multi-layer perceptron. B-NDRA achieved an average AUC of 92.2% in five-fold cross-validation, validated through case studies on doxorubicin and imatinib, highlighting its potential for cancer research and therapeutic development.

In addition to these, other recent computational methods have been proposed to explore the associations between miRNA, circRNA, lncRNA, and drug resistance. Huang et al. [10] introduced GCMDR, which frames miRNA-drug resistance prediction as a link prediction problem in a bipartite graph, using graph convolution to integrate high-dimensional miRNA and drug attributes. Niu et al. [11] developed AMMGC, an attention-driven multimodal graph convolutional framework that captures hidden representations of drugs and miRNAs using graph convolution modules, and applies attention mechanisms to infer associations through inner product operations. Chen et al. [12] introduced NNHLDA, a method that incorporates neighborhood information to predict lncRNA-disease associations, highlighting its potential through gastric cancer case studies. Cao et al. [13] introduced GGCDA, a framework for predicting circRNA-disease relationships using GAT, GCN, and multiple similarity types, enhanced by random walk with restart (RWR) and multi-layer neural networks. Zeng et al. [14] introduced a similar GGCDA method, utilizing multi-head GAT and GCN to predict circRNA-disease associations. Xuan et al. [15] developed CNNMDA, which predicts disease-related miRNAs by integrating miRNA-disease similarity and associations in a low-dimensional space. Liu et al. [16] developed GraphCDD, which predicts circRNA-drug resistance associations by integrating circRNA, disease, and drug data using multimodal graph neural networks.

Despite accumulating evidence that ncRNAs contribute to drug resistance, several challenges remain. Few models are tailored to predict drug resistance–associated ncRNAs, and most focus on a single ncRNA type. Many methods also underutilize the rich information in ncRNA sequences, limiting their ability to capture sequence complexity and cross-type relationships. In addition, current models often represent ncRNAs and small-molecule drugs using only a single feature view, with insufficient multi-view or multi-scale integration, which restricts predictive performance. Finally, their limited capability in identifying drug resistance–associated ncRNAs (NDRAs) further hampers advances in drug resistance prediction and mechanistic insight.

To address the challenge of predicting drug resistance–associated ncRNAs, we propose MIFNDRA (Fig. 1), a multimodal, knowledge-enhanced graph learning framework for ncRNA–drug resistance association prediction. MIFNDRA models drug semantic similarity using a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG) with semantic contribution decay, and derives ncRNA functional similarity from their associated drugs, which is further refined via Gaussian Interaction Profile (GIP) kernel fusion to construct unified similarity representations for ncRNAs and drugs. Drug molecular structures and ncRNA sequences are encoded using a pre-trained Graph Isomorphism Network (GIN) and SpliceBERT, respectively. In addition, a comprehensive ncRNA interaction network integrating validated interactions and sequence similarity is incorporated to capture higher-order ncRNA relationships. Building on these representations, MIFNDRA employs a residual GraphSAGE architecture with contrastive learning to enhance representation discrimination, substantially improving the identification of drug resistance–associated ncRNAs (NDRAs). Moreover, we construct a novel ncRNA–drug resistance dataset integrating multiple ncRNA types and drug SMILES representations. Extensive experiments on benchmark and newly constructed datasets demonstrate that MIFNDRA achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance.

caption.p: Overview of the MIFNDRA framework for ncRNA–drug resistance association prediction. (a) Drug SMILES and ncRNA sequences are collected from multiple databases to build drug/ncRNA feature graphs via KNN and an association (resistance) graph from known links; all three graphs are fed into the learning and prediction modules. (b) Drug multimodal feature fusion module: Drug semantic similarity, GIP kernel similarity, and GIN-derived molecular structural embeddings are integrated and then projected by PCA to obtain unified drug representations. (c) ncRNA multimodal feature fusion module: SpliceBERT embeddings, GIP similarity, functional similarity, and knowledge-enhanced interaction-network features are fused, followed by PCA to obtain unified ncRNA embeddings. (d) ncRNA interaction network: Validated ncRNA interactions are integrated to form the network, with edges weighted by smith–waterman similarity (validated edges set to 1) and attention-guided walks to capture higher-order relations. (e) Graph learning module: Res-GraphSAGE encodes the drug, ncRNA, and resistance graphs, followed by global and nonlinear adaptive fusion. (f) Prediction module: An MLP predicts association scores, optimized with weighted triplet and prediction losses ().

sec.title: Dataset construction and preprocessing
sec.p: In this study, two datasets were used. Dataset 1 was constructed by Zhang et al. [9] based on the NcDR [17] and NoncoRNA [18] databases, yielding 2682 known ncRNA–drug resistance association (NDRA) pairs involving 116 drugs and multiple ncRNA types, including miRNAs, lncRNAs, and circRNAs (Table 1). Although this dataset provides a valuable benchmark, it lacks ncRNA sequence information and contains relatively limited data, which constrains its applicability for comprehensive modeling of ncRNA–drug resistance mechanisms.

caption.p: Composition and statistics of the datasets used in this study.

sec.p: To address these limitations, we constructed a more comprehensive Dataset 2 by integrating known NDRA pairs from the ncRNADrug database [19], newly reported associations curated from PubMed [20], and additional ncRNA categories, including piRNAs. ncRNA sequence data were collected from miRBase [21], NCBI [22], circBase [23], and piRBase [24], while drug structural information in the form of SMILES was obtained from DrugBank [25]. As summarized in Table 1, Dataset 2 contains 7432 ncRNA–drug resistance association pairs, involving 3 piRNAs, 723 circRNAs, 1250 lncRNAs, 1346 miRNAs, and 121 drugs. Moreover, in Dataset 2, experimentally supported ncRNA–ncRNA interactions were curated from the literature in PubMed [20] to enrich network-level information, including 302 miRNA–circRNA, 134 lncRNA–miRNA, and 2 lncRNA–circRNA interaction pairs. To our knowledge, Dataset 2 represents the first ncRNA–drug resistance dataset that simultaneously integrates ncRNA sequence features, drug structural information, and ncRNA interaction networks, providing a multidimensional resource for investigating ncRNA-mediated drug resistance.

sec.title: GIN for drug structural feature representation
sec.p: The GIN is a specialized graph neural network designed to effectively represent graph structures through unsupervised learning techniques [28]. In our research, GIN serves as the backbone for encoding the structural properties of drugs. We employed a pre-trained GIN model available from DGLLifeSci [29], which has been fine-tuned to capture the nuanced structural nuances of various drug molecules. This pre-trained model provides robust feature representations that facilitate the accurate prediction of associations between ncRNAs and drug resistance mechanisms.

Here, and denote the feature vectors of node and its neighboring node from the -th layer, respectively. The scalar parameter controls the relative importance of the central node’s own feature with respect to the aggregated features of its neighboring nodes at the -th layer. The role of is to map the aggregated features into a new feature space, effectively capturing complex non-linear relationships within the graph. Through this mechanism, GIN is capable of generating highly expressive node features, enhancing the model's ability to distinguish between different graph structures and node roles.

sec.title: SpliceBERT for ncRNA sequence feature extraction
sec.p: SpliceBERT [30] is a BERT-based deep learning model [31] developed for predicting and analyzing RNA splicing events. In this study, we use SpliceBERT to extract informative features from ncRNA sequences, capturing complex sequence patterns and contextual dependencies to strengthen ncRNA–drug resistance association prediction. SpliceBERT is self-supervisedly pre-trained with masked language modeling [32] on over two million RNA sequences from 72 vertebrate species, enabling it to learn evolutionarily conserved signals. It produces nucleotide-level embeddings and attention weights; the embeddings summarize sequence information, while the self-attention mechanism models long-range dependencies, facilitating the identification of functional regions and conserved sites within ncRNAs.

sec.title: Knowledge augmentation through ncRNA interconnections
sec.p: To move beyond conventional approaches that rely primarily on first-order ncRNA–drug associations, we incorporated multi-type ncRNA interconnections (lncRNAs, circRNAs, and miRNAs) by constructing an integrated ncRNA interaction network that models both direct and indirect relationships. In this network, literature- or experiment-supported interactions were assigned an edge weight of 1, whereas previously unreported associations were weighted according to Smith–Waterman local alignment–based sequence similarity [33]. During graph representation learning, we adopted an Attention-guided Walk mechanism [34] to dynamically emphasize informative neighbors and paths, enabling the model to capture higher-order connectivity and thereby improve the identification of drug-resistance–associated ncRNAs (details and formulations are provided in the Supplementary Material Section S1 available online at http://bib.oxfordjournals.org/).

sec.title: Multimodal feature fusion module
sec.p: In this study, we propose a multimodal feature fusion module within a unified graph-learning framework to integrate heterogeneous information from drugs and ncRNAs, thereby learning more discriminative node representations for association prediction. For drugs, we compute structural similarity using RDKit fingerprints with the Tanimoto coefficient (Section 2.2.1), semantic similarity via DAG-based propagation (Section 2.2.2), and interaction-profile similarity using the GIP kernel (Section 2.2.4), which are fused into a drug similarity matrix . In addition, a pretrained GIN encoder (Section 2.3.1) is used to generate molecular graph embeddings that enrich drug representations. For ncRNAs, functional similarity (Section 2.2.3) and GIP similarity (Section 2.2.4) are fused into , and SpliceBERT embeddings (Section 2.3.2) are incorporated to capture contextual and long-range sequence dependencies. Meanwhile, the ncRNA interaction network built from literature evidence and Smith–Waterman weighted sequence similarity (Section 2.4) is embedded using an Attention-guided Walk to obtain knowledge-enhanced higher-order representations that capture direct and indirect relations as well as potential regulatory paths. Finally, drug representations are formed by concatenating fused similarities with GIN embeddings, whereas ncRNA representations are obtained by concatenating fused similarities, SpliceBERT embeddings, and network embeddings, providing a robust basis for inferring ncRNA–drug resistance associations.

sec.title: Graph learning module
sec.p: Leveraging the learned multimodal representations of drugs and ncRNAs, we construct a drug multimodal feature graph and an ncRNA multimodal feature graph, which are then processed by graph neural networks for representation learning. For each unimodal graph, we define a node feature matrix and build the graph structure using a similarity-based neighborhood strategy. Specifically, we apply PCA to the node feature matrix to reduce dimensionality and ensure consistent input size for subsequent graph learning. We then use the K-nearest neighbors (KNN) rule to generate the adjacency matrix, connecting each node to its K most similar neighbors. For the ncRNA–drug resistance association graph, the adjacency matrix is directly derived from known ncRNA–drug resistance associations. We adopt GraphSAGE to learn graph-aware node representations by aggregating neighborhood information and combining it with the node’s own features. To alleviate performance degradation caused by over-smoothing during deeper propagation, we incorporate residual connections into GraphSAGE and denote the resulting model as Res-GraphSAGE. To comprehensively model drug–ncRNA interactions, three parallel Res-GraphSAGE encoders are employed to process the drug graph, ncRNA graph, and ncRNA–drug resistance graph, respectively, and are trained jointly.

After graph encoding, we introduce a nonlinear fusion module that adaptively merges paired feature vectors via an attention-like gating mechanism, and further integrates a global context vector to enhance generalization. The fused representations are finally fed into an MLP with a Sigmoid output to produce association scores between ncRNAs and drug resistance. Detailed constructions, equations, and fusion formulations are provided in the Supplementary Material Section S2 available online at http://bib.oxfordjournals.org/.

sec.title: Experimental environment and hyperparameter settings
sec.p: The experiments were conducted on an NVIDIA A800 GPU (80 GB PCIe) with Ubuntu 18.04. The hyperparameters of the MIFNDRA model were carefully tuned through systematic exploration. Initially, the number of training epochs was fixed at 60. We then fine-tuned the learning rate across 0.1, 0.01, 0.001, and 0.0001, ultimately determining that 0.0001 yielded the best results. The dropout rate was tested at 0.1, 0.3, 0.5, and 0.7, with 0.3 providing the most stable performance. Similarly, weight decay coefficients were examined over values of 1e-2, 5e-3, 5e-5, and 1e-6, where 1e-6 achieved the optimal balance between generalization and convergence. Through these evaluations, the final hyperparameter configuration of 60 training epochs, a learning rate of 0.0001, a dropout rate of 0.3, and a weight decay of 1e-6 was shown to deliver the best performance for the MIFNDRA model.

sec.title: Model performance evaluation
sec.p: We conducted five-fold cross-validation on Dataset 1 and Dataset 2 to evaluate the performance of MIFNDRA. Owing to the absence of ncRNA–ncRNA interaction data and ncRNA sequence information in Dataset 1, the model relied only on ncRNA similarity features and multimodal drug features, without sequence features or interaction-based knowledge augmentation, thereby reflecting a data-scarce setting. As summarized in Supplementary Table S1 in Supplementary Section S3, MIFNDRA achieved strong performance on Dataset 1, with a mean AUC of 0.9529 ± 0.0115 and an accuracy of 0.8934 ± 0.0150, demonstrating robust predictive capability under limited data conditions. Performance further improved on Dataset 2, as shown in Supplementary Table S2 in Supplementary Section S3, yielding a mean AUC of 0.9685 ± 0.0013 and an accuracy of 0.9314 ± 0.0206, along with consistently high AUPRC, F1-score, recall, and precision. The ROC and precision–recall curves in Supplementary Fig. S1 in Supplementary Section S3 show that fold-specific curves cluster tightly around the mean curves for both datasets, indicating high stability and robustness of MIFNDRA across different data settings and evaluation metrics.

sec.title: Comparison with existing leading models
sec.p: In this section, we compare MIFNDRA with five benchmark methods (GAEMDA, GRPMDA, LRGCPND, GraphCDD, and the SOTA B-NDRA) under five-fold cross-validation on Dataset 1. As shown in Table 2, MIFNDRA consistently outperforms all competing methods across six evaluation metrics. It achieves accuracy improvements of 4.46%–10.01%, F1-score gains of 4.27%–11.84%, and recall increases of 9.38%–18.29% over the baselines, while maintaining highly competitive precision, indicating effective control of false positives. In addition, MIFNDRA delivers AUC improvements of 3.09%–9.63% and AUPRC gains of 2.28%–7.39%, demonstrating superior discriminative ability and robustness under class imbalance. These advantages are further reflected in the ROC and precision–recall curves shown in Fig. 2a and b, where MIFNDRA consistently encloses the performance of all baseline methods. Overall, these results confirm the significant and consistent superiority of MIFNDRA on Dataset 1.

sec.p: Under five-fold cross-validation on Dataset 2, MIFNDRA consistently outperformed all five SOTA baselines across all evaluation metrics (Table 3). It achieved an accuracy of 0.9384, with improvements of 3.31%–7.61% over competing methods, while also delivering superior F1-score (0.9323), recall (0.9444), and precision (0.9207). Moreover, MIFNDRA exhibited strong discriminative ability, attaining an AUC of 0.9685 and an AUPRC of 0.9540, surpassing all baselines by notable margins. These advantages are further confirmed by the ROC and precision–recall curves in Fig. 2c and d. In addition, MIFNDRA also showed superior calibration performance in terms of the Brier Score (Supplementary Section S4 available online at http://bib.oxfordjournals.org/, Table S3 available online at http://bib.oxfordjournals.org/), achieving the lowest values on both Dataset 1 (0.0884 ± 0.0066) and Dataset 2 (0.0607 ± 0.0039). Overall, the consistent gains across all metrics demonstrate the robustness and strong generalization capability of MIFNDRA on both Dataset 2 and the more data-limited Dataset 1, while highlighting its adaptability to datasets with different scales and information richness and its ability to provide more reliable probability estimates under class-imbalanced conditions.

sec.title: Ablation study and component effect analysis
Impact of multimodal feature fusion on model performance
sec.p: In this study, we evaluated the effect of progressive multimodal feature fusion by constructing four MIFNDRA variants with increasing complexity. On Dataset 1 (Table 4), the baseline MIFNDRA-sim, using only similarity-based features, achieved an accuracy of 0.8707 and an F1-score of 0.8835. Incorporating drug structural features (MIFNDRA-ssf) led to consistent improvements across all metrics, including noticeable gains in accuracy, F1-score, recall, and ranking-based measures (AUC and AUPRC). As ncRNA sequence information is unavailable in Dataset 1, MIFNDRA-ssf represents the final configuration under this setting.

caption.p: Performance comparison of multimodal feature fusion on dataset 1.

sec.p: On Dataset 2 (Table 5), MIFNDRA-sim already showed strong performance (accuracy >0.92, AUC = 0.9610), which was further enhanced by introducing structural features. Additional incorporation of ncRNA sequence features (MIFNDRA-nsf) yielded further improvements, particularly in accuracy and F1-score. The fully integrated model, MIFNDRA-ful, achieved the best overall performance, with an accuracy of 0.9384, an F1-score of 0.9323, and the highest AUC and AUPRC values. Overall, these results demonstrate a clear and consistent performance gain with each added feature modality, among which network topology–based information contributes most substantially, highlighting its critical role in modeling complex biological relationships.

caption.p: Performance comparison of multimodal feature fusion on dataset 2.

sec.title: Impact of knowledge enhancement on model performance
sec.p: This section investigates the effect of incorporating ncRNA interaction networks as a knowledge enhancement strategy. Four variants of MIFNDRA were designed: the baseline MIFNDRA-bas using only original multimodal features; MIFNDRA-mla incorporating miRNA–lncRNA interactions; MIFNDRA-mca further integrating miRNA–circRNA interactions; and MIFNDRA-all combining miRNA–lncRNA, miRNA–circRNA, and lncRNA–circRNA interactions to capture more comprehensive network patterns. All experiments were conducted on Dataset 2 using five-fold cross-validation.

As shown in Fig. 3, model performance consistently improved with the progressive incorporation of interaction information. Compared with the baseline, introducing miRNA–lncRNA interactions enhanced accuracy and recall, while further adding miRNA–circRNA interactions led to additional gains in accuracy, F1-score, and precision. The fully integrated model, MIFNDRA-all, achieved the best overall performance, with an accuracy of 0.9384, an F1-score of 0.9323, a recall of 0.9444, a precision of 0.9207, and the highest AUC (0.9685) and AUPRC (0.9540). Overall, these results demonstrate that progressively enriched ncRNA interaction networks effectively improve predictive accuracy and generalization, highlighting the value of knowledge enhancement for ncRNA-associated drug resistance prediction.

caption.p: Performance comparison of models with different ncRNA interaction networks. MIFNDRA-bas denotes the baseline model using only original multimodal features; MIFNDRA-mla incorporates known miRNA–lncRNA interaction information; MIFNDRA-mca further integrates miRNA–circRNA interactions based on MIFNDRA-mla; and MIFNDRA-all incorporates miRNA–lncRNA, miRNA–circRNA, and lncRNA–circRNA interactions to capture comprehensive ncRNA interaction network patterns.

graphic.alt-text: Line chart comparing the performance of MIFNDRA variants using different ncRNA interaction networks, including baseline, miRNA--lncRNA, miRNA--circRNA, and complete ncRNA interaction settings.

sec.title: Ablation experiments on the graph learning module
sec.p: To assess the contribution of individual components in the graph learning module of MIFNDRA, we conducted ablation experiments on Dataset 2 using five-fold cross-validation. Three variant models were evaluated: MIFNDRA-nnf, which replaces the non-linear adaptive fusion with direct feature fusion; MIFNDRA-ngl, which removes the global fusion module; and MIFNDRA-nts, which excludes the triplet contrastive loss. As shown in Fig. 4, removing or simplifying any component led to performance degradation. MIFNDRA-nnf exhibited the most pronounced decline (ACC = 0.9129, AUC = 0.9553), indicating the importance of non-linear adaptive fusion. MIFNDRA-ngl achieved slightly better results (ACC = 0.9289, AUC = 0.9667), while MIFNDRA-nts showed moderate decreases in accuracy and discriminative ability (ACC = 0.9223, AUC = 0.9657). In contrast, the full MIFNDRA model consistently outperformed all variants, achieving the best performance (ACC = 0.9384, AUC = 0.9685). These results confirm that non-linear adaptive fusion, global fusion, and contrastive learning jointly contribute to the superior predictive performance of MIFNDRA.

caption.p: Five-fold cross-validation ablation study of MIFNDRA modules on dataset 2. MIFNDRA-nnf replaces the non-linear adaptive fusion mechanism in the graph learning module with a direct connection-based fusion; MIFNDRA-ngl removes the global fusion module; MIFNDRA-nts excludes the triple contrastive loss and is trained using only the classification loss; and MIFNDRA denotes the full model incorporating all proposed components.

sec.title: Performance under different sample ratios
sec.p: We evaluated the performance of MIFNDRA under varying positive-to-negative sample ratios (1:1, 1:2, 1:5, and 1:10) to assess its robustness to class imbalance (Fig. 5). The model achieved the best performance under the balanced 1:1 setting (ACC = 0.9384, F1 = 0.9323, AUC = 0.9685, AUPRC = 0.9540). As imbalance increased, accuracy and F1-score gradually declined, whereas recall and AUPRC remained relatively stable, indicating effective detection of minority samples. At extreme imbalance (1:10), recall, precision, and F1-score dropped noticeably, suggesting reduced reliability under highly skewed distributions. Overall, MIFNDRA demonstrated strong robustness to moderate class imbalance, maintaining stable discriminative ability (AUC) and comparatively high recall. Performance improved markedly as the data became more balanced, highlighting the model’s effectiveness for drug resistance–related ncRNA prediction and its potential value for downstream experimental validation.

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis to key hyperparameter
sec.p: We conducted a sensitivity analysis of key hyperparameters for MIFNDRA on Dataset 2 using five-fold cross-validation, including the embedding dimension, GraphSAGE depth, neighborhood size , and the loss balance coefficient . As shown in Fig. 6, increasing the embedding dimension from 64 to 128 led to clear performance improvements, with accuracy increasing from 0.9180 to 0.9384, AUC from 0.9600 to 0.9685, and AUPRC from 0.9460 to 0.9540, whereas a further increase to 256 resulted in slight degradation. A three-layer GraphSAGE architecture achieved the best results (ACC = 0.9384, AUC = 0.9685), outperforming both shallower and deeper variants. Similarly, =20 yielded optimal performance, while =10 or 30 caused minor declines. Regarding loss balancing, =0.6 provided the most effective trade-off between binary cross-entropy and triplet contrastive loss, outperforming other settings. Overall, the optimal hyperparameter configuration for MIFNDRA consists of an embedding dimension of 128, three GraphSAGE layers, =20, and =0.6.

sec.title: Case study
sec.p: To further evaluate the practical utility of MIFNDRA, we conducted case studies on two representative anticancer drugs, Cisplatin and Gemcitabine, to examine whether the model could successfully prioritize ncRNAs potentially associated with drug resistance. Cisplatin is a widely used platinum-based chemotherapeutic agent for the treatment of various malignancies, including ovarian, lung, bladder, testicular, and head and neck cancers. Its antitumor activity mainly arises from the formation of platinum-DNA adducts, which interfere with DNA replication and repair and ultimately induce apoptosis [36, 37]. Gemcitabine is a nucleoside analog widely used for pancreatic cancer, non-small cell lung cancer, bladder cancer, and breast cancer. It disrupts DNA synthesis and repair by mimicking deoxynucleotides, thereby inhibiting cancer cell proliferation and inducing cell death [38].

For each case study, all known drug–ncRNA associations related to the target drug were excluded from training and treated as the test set, while the remaining known drug–ncRNA resistance associations were used as the training set, following the experimental setting of B-NDRA [9]. The same procedure was applied to both Cisplatin and Gemcitabine. After training, the model generated a prediction score for each candidate ncRNA with respect to the target drug, reflecting the likelihood that the ncRNA is associated with drug resistance. The candidate ncRNAs were then ranked in descending order according to their predicted scores, and the top 20 were selected for further validation through PubMed literature. As shown in Table 6, 18 of the top 20 ncRNAs predicted for Cisplatin were supported by published studies. For example, exosomes derived from M2-polarized macrophages were reported to promote Cisplatin (DDP) resistance in gastric cancer cells through the transfer of hsa-miR-588 [39]. Similarly, for Gemcitabine, 17 of the top 20 predicted ncRNAs were validated by PubMed evidence, as shown in Table 7. For instance, miR-130a-3p has been reported to target PPARG and to be associated with Gemcitabine resistance in cholangiocarcinoma (CCA) [40]. These results demonstrate that MIFNDRA can effectively prioritize biologically meaningful ncRNA candidates related to drug resistance. To facilitate a direct comparison with the original B-NDRA study, we additionally evaluated MIFNDRA on Doxorubicin and Imatinib under the same data construction setting, as shown in Supplementary Section S5, including Supplementary Tables S4 and S5. For both drugs, 18 of the top 20 predicted ncRNAs were validated by PubMed literature, compared with 16 of the top 20 reported in the original B-NDRA study. These supplementary results further support the robust predictive capability of MIFNDRA.

It is worth noting that these case study results are not limited to miRNAs. As shown in Tables 6 and 7, several top-ranked candidates belong to other ncRNA classes, including lncRNAs and circRNAs, suggesting that MIFNDRA is capable of identifying drug resistance-related ncRNAs across multiple categories. To further extend this analysis, we provide additional results in Supplementary Section S6, including Supplementary Tables S6 and S7, where predicted cisplatin resistance-associated lncRNAs and circRNAs are presented, with the majority of these candidates supported by existing literature. Furthermore, Supplementary Table S8 in Supplementary Section S7 introduces a mechanism-oriented cross-class subnetwork recovery analysis, which illustrates the ability of MIFNDRA to capture heterogeneous regulatory patterns among different ncRNA types in the context of drug resistance.

Through this process, we have demonstrated the effectiveness of the MIFNDRA model in identifying ncRNAs associated with Cisplatin and Gemcitabine, further advancing research into drug resistance mechanisms.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: ncRNAs are closely linked to cancer drug resistance, but their mechanisms are still not fully understood and existing computational approaches remain limited. In this work, we introduce MIFNDRA, a multimodal model that uses pre-trained GIN and SpliceBERT to capture drug structural information and ncRNA sequence features. The framework incorporates various similarity features for both drugs and ncRNAs, and further boosts representation learning through an ncRNA interaction network, residual GraphSAGE, and contrastive learning. We also build a new ncRNA–drug resistance dataset, on which MIFNDRA delivers SOTA results, further supported by case studies on cisplatin and gemcitabine.

Despite the success of the MIFNDRA model, challenges remain, including the scarcity of high-quality labeled data for ncRNAs involved in drug resistance. While a new dataset has been created, it still requires further refinement and validation. The model's reliance on predefined similarity metrics may not fully capture the complexity of ncRNA–drug interactions, and its performance could be influenced by biological data heterogeneity, such as varying ncRNA expression across different conditions. Future research should focus on expanding the dataset, incorporating more complex molecular interactions, and exploring hybrid models for improved robustness and accuracy.

list-item.p: This study proposes MIFNDRA, a multimodal framework that integrates pre-trained Graph Isomorphism Network and SpliceBERT features with drug/ncRNA similarity information, and enhances representations via an ncRNA interaction network plus residual GraphSAGE and contrastive learning to improve identification of drug resistance–associated ncRNAs.
A new ncRNA–drug resistance dataset was built from public databases and PubMed literature, including ncRNA sequences, drug SMILES, and ncRNA interaction data to provide a unified resource.
Experiments on benchmark and newly constructed datasets show MIFNDRA achieves improved performance and state-of-the-art results, demonstrating strong potential for drug resistance research.
